newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan official sees possible North Korea collapse.
newsitem.headline: Japan official sees possible North Korea collapse.

text.p: The defection of a top North Korean official could set off a power struggle that would lead to more defections, a refugee flight and the ultimate collapse of the communist nation, a senior Japanese government official said on Thursday.

As ripples from the defection spread, Japan dusted off its contingency plans for a North Korean crisis that included scenarios ranging from a refugee exodus to a last gasp military strike by the tottering Stalinist administration.
The cause of the turmoil was Hwang Jang-yop, 72, a senior adviser to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, who on Wednesday sought asylum at the South Korean embassy in Beijing.
"We really don't know if Hwang's defection was a by-product of a power struggle," the official told Reuters.

"But now everyone in North Korea's ruling structure is going to be suspicious of everyone else, as well as their own future, and that could prompt a really destructive power struggle," said the official, who spoke on condition he was not identified.
The official is one of the Japanese government's top experts on North Korean affairs with access to intelligence on developments in the communist country.
He said Kim's promotion last week of six young army officers to posts around him was another unsettling development for old-time party members like Hwang and could add to the turmoil.
He said the cash-strapped Stalinist state, gripped by famine after two consecutive years of flooding, appears to have taken the first step towards self-destruction.

"North Korea is definitely in the process of collapsing. The end could happen tomorrow or five years from now. Who predicted the collapse of the Berlin Wall one week ahead of time?" the official said.
"But the country is definitely at the terminal stage."
He forecast the first fallout from the defection could be a delay in Kim Jong-il's formal accession to power.

Kim, supreme commander of the country's 1.1-million-strong military, has yet to be formally confirmed in two key posts held by his late father Kim Il-sung -- general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party and state president.
Korea-watchers believed Kim would assume the posts shortly after the third anniversary of his father's death in July 1994.
"But with this defection, it is becoming doubtful if Kim Jong-il can control the country," the official said.
Hwang's defection, and what it said about support for Kim, could also threaten ties with North Korea's main ally China.
"If China turns its back, North Korea has lost the survival game," the official said.

He argued that without the backing of China, there was no reason for North Korea to take part in four-nation talks -- involving China, the United States, South Korea and North Korea -- aimed at a permanent peace on the Korean Peninsula.
North Korea was to attend a briefing on the proposal this month but has twice delayed the meeting.
"If it felt itself isolated, North Korea could decide to retreat even further from the world," the official said.
He said an even worse possibility was a desperate North Korea deciding it had nothing to lose and resorting to a military provocation against the South.
"We should not rule out a worst-case scenario where North Korea could be driven to desperation," the official said.
